tool_config.title: Unit Picker
tool_config.screen: The long cloth table of the village weaving centre, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, with a measuring tape running along the top of the wall. A picture card of a thing (a pencil, a classroom door, a school bus, a postage stamp, a handkerchief) stands on the table as the largest object on screen, with a number tag beside it, for example 17. Under the card are two unit tags, cm and m, to drag onto the number tag. A tape strip along the wall draws the length as a bar for the chosen unit, with a 1 m mark and a 1 cm mark always shown, so a wrong unit makes the bar run far past the picture or shrink to a dot. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the cm tag or the m tag onto the number tag; tap the tag again to take it off; in the rule card, drag the unit cards cm and m into two gaps; answer tags for the book's questions; Check, Hint, Retry (takes the tag off this card), Reset (returns all cards), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the number with its unit under the picture, the bar on the wall tape, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: A tag dropped on a number draws a bar on the wall tape. If the bar runs far past the picture, the tool says, for example: 17 m is longer than a classroom, but a pencil is small. Try the other tag.
If the bar shrinks to a dot, the tool says, for example: 2 cm is a tiny length, but a door is tall. Try the other tag.
A tag that fits locks in with a soft chime and the bar turns green, with the words: 17 cm fits the pencil.
In the book's questions the bar is drawn after the student has chosen a unit, and the tool says whether the length is sensible, in the same plain words.
A wrong rule card slides back with a clue such as: Think of a pencil. Is it short or long?
tool_config.done_when: All four picture cards have the right tag, the rule is finished, and all six lengths of Let Us Find have a unit.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): a pencil with the number 17. Drop m, then cm, and watch the bar. Answer: cm, because 17 cm fits the pencil and 17 m would be longer than a classroom.
Card 2 (practice values): a classroom door with the number 2. Answer: m, because a door is taller than a child, so 2 m fits, and 2 cm is a tiny length.
Card 3 (practice values): a school bus with the number 9. Answer: m, because a bus is long and 9 cm would be shorter than a pencil.
Card 4 (practice values): a postage stamp with the number 3. Answer: cm, because a stamp is tiny and 3 m would be longer than a door.
Card 5: finish the rule with the unit cards. Short things are measured in ___ and long things in ___. Answer: cm, then m.

Challenge: 'Identify the appropriate units for measuring each of the following.' (a) the height of India Gate is 42, (b) the length of a handkerchief is 40, (c) the depth of a well is 50. Choose m or cm for each. Answer: 42 m, 40 cm and 50 m.

Challenge: (d) the length of a mobile phone is 13, (e) the length of an elephant's trunk is 2, (f) the distance between two buttons on a shirt is 5. Choose m or cm for each. Answer: 13 cm, 2 m and 5 cm. Next stop: how one length has two names.

The tool drops the right tag on this card: cm for a thing that fits in your hand, m for a thing as long as a room or longer.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: Shikha's tape says 300 and Sonu's tape says 3 for the same stole. Can both numbers be right? Yes. The two tapes use different units. 1 m is the same length as 100 cm, so one length has two names. A double number line shows both names. The top line is in m, the bottom line is in cm, and from the top line to the bottom line every number is multiplied by 100. To change m to cm, multiply by 100: 3 m = 3 × 100 = 300 cm. To change cm to m and cm, take out the hundreds: 450 cm = 400 cm + 50 cm = 4 m 50 cm, because 400 ÷ 100 = 4. A part bigger than 100 cm is allowed too: 3 m 130 cm = 300 cm + 130 cm = 430 cm. Rule: 1 m = 100 cm, so multiply by 100 to change m to cm. 1. 1 m = 100 cm, so change m to cm by multiplying by 100. 2. 3 m = 3 × 100 = 300 cm. 3. To change 450 cm, take out the hundreds: 450 cm = 400 cm + 50 cm. 4. 400 cm = 400 ÷ 100 = 4 m, so 450 cm = 4 m 50 cm. 5. Check: 4 m 50 cm = 4 × 100 + 50 = 450 cm. Answer: 3 m = 300 cm and 450 cm = 4 m 50 cm

1. Predict first: Shikha's tape says 300 and Sonu's tape says 3 for the same stole. Can both numbers be right?
2. Yes. The two tapes use different units. 1 m is the same length as 100 cm, so one length has two names.

4. To change m to cm, multiply by 100: 3 m = 3 × 100 = 300 cm.
5. To change cm to m and cm, take out the hundreds: 450 cm = 400 cm + 50 cm = 4 m 50 cm, because 400 ÷ 100 = 4.
6. A part bigger than 100 cm is allowed too: 3 m 130 cm = 300 cm + 130 cm = 430 cm.
7. Rule: 1 m = 100 cm, so multiply by 100 to change m to cm.

concepts.concept_name: Different Units but Same Measure: Q1

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S4.T4.C9.IMG1}}
1. The top line is in cm and the bottom line is in m. The arrow $\times 100$ says that m become cm when you multiply by $100$.
2. The arrow $\times 2$ says that $2\text{ m}$ is twice $1\text{ m}$, so the cm are twice $100\text{ cm}$: $2 \times 100 = 200\text{ cm}$. The first blank is $200\text{ cm}$.
3. $400\text{ cm}$ is $400 \div 100 = 4\text{ m}$, so the first blank on the bottom line is $4\text{ m}$.
4. $500\text{ cm}$ is $500 \div 100 = 5\text{ m}$, so the next blank is $5\text{ m}$.
5. $700\text{ cm}$ is $700 \div 100 = 7\text{ m}$, so the last blank is $7\text{ m}$.
[Image: Different Units but Same Measure: Ans1: solution]
6. Check: $4 \times 100 = 400$, $5 \times 100 = 500$ and $7 \times 100 = 700$.
Answer: Top line: $200\text{ cm}$. Bottom line: $4\text{ m}$, $5\text{ m}$, $7\text{ m}$
[Image: Different Units but Same Measure: Ans1: solution (continued)]
steps: The top line is in cm and the bottom line is in m. The arrow ×100 says that m become cm when you multiply by 100.
The arrow ×2 says that 2 m is twice 1 m, so the cm are twice 100 cm: 2 × 100 = 200 cm. The first blank is 200 cm.
400 cm is 400 ÷ 100 = 4 m, so the first blank on the bottom line is 4 m.

tool_config.idea: Compare two lengths given in different units by changing both to one unit, and read the difference as the gap between two bars on one tape. A doubled bar helps find the length that doubles to a given length.
tool_config.title: Length Bars
tool_config.screen: The weaving centre's long wall tape in cm, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, with rods and lengths of cloth hung along it. Two bars sit on one tape, drawn to scale, and they are the largest things on screen; each bar has a length card in its own units, for example 4 m 3 cm. A Change to cm button under each card shows the working, for example 4 × 100 + 3 = 403, and the card turns into cm. A sign box between the bars takes the signs <, = and >. A gap marker appears between the ends of the bars and shows the difference when both are in cm. A Double button stretches a bar to twice its length. In the statue stage the six statues of your maths book stand as bars on one base line (182 m, 128 m, 108 m, 93 m, 91 m and 38 m), and tapping two statues puts their bars side by side with the gap. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: Change to cm on each card; drag a sign into the sign box; tap two statues; Double; type an answer into a box; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the sign and the conversion of this card), Reset (restores all bars), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: each length in its own units and in cm, the gap in cm, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: Change to cm shows the working on the card, for example 4 × 100 + 3 = 403, and the bar redraws in cm. If the two lengths are still in different units, the tool says: Change both to the same unit first.
A sign dropped in the sign box is checked against the two numbers in cm and the tool says why, for example: 403 is less than 430, so the sign is <.
The gap marker shows the difference in cm only when both bars are in cm, and the tool says: The difference is the longer bar minus the shorter bar.
The Double button stretches a bar, and a bar of the same length lights up in green; if none matches, the tool says: Halve the long bar to find the short one.
In the statue stage, two tapped statues show their heights side by side and the gap, and the tool says whether the gap is the least or the largest only after the student has tried the pairs.
tool_config.done_when: All five practice cards are solved, the five rod comparisons have signs, and the four statue questions are answered.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): compare 4 m 3 cm and 430 cm. Change both to cm and drop a sign. Answer: 4 m 3 cm = 4 × 100 + 3 = 403 cm, and 403 < 430, so 4 m 3 cm < 430 cm.
Card 2 (practice values): compare 3 m 20 cm and 300 cm + 20 cm. Answer: 3 m 20 cm = 320 cm and 300 cm + 20 cm = 320 cm, so they are equal.
Card 3 (practice values): find the gap between 3 m 45 cm and 290 cm. Answer: 3 m 45 cm = 345 cm and 345 − 290 = 55 cm.
Card 4 (practice values): double a bar of 85 cm and find which of the bars 60 cm, 170 cm and 255 cm is the same length as the doubled bar. Answer: 85 × 2 = 170 cm, so the bar of 170 cm.

Card 5 (practice values): put three bars in order from the shortest to the longest after changing them to cm: 2 m 5 cm, 190 cm and 2 m 50 cm. Answer: 2 m 5 cm = 205 cm and 2 m 50 cm = 250 cm, so the order is 190 cm, 2 m 5 cm, 2 m 50 cm.

Challenge: 'Ritika is comparing the lengths of different rods. Compare them using <, =, > signs.' (a) 456 cm and 5 m; (b) 55 cm + 200 cm and 200 cm + 54 cm; (c) 6 m 5 cm and 6 m 50 cm; (d) 2 m 150 cm and 3 m 50 cm; (e) 238 cm and 138 cm + 1 m. Answer: (a) <; (b) >; (c) <; (d) =; (e) =.

Challenge: the world's tallest statues, with the heights 182 m, 128 m, 108 m, 93 m, 91 m and 38 m: (a) the difference between the height of the tallest statue and the Statue of Liberty; (b) the statues whose heights have the least difference; (c) the statues whose heights have the largest difference; (d) the statue whose height doubled is the height of the Statue of Unity. Answer: (a) 182 − 93 = 89 m; (b) the Statue of Liberty and The Motherland Calls, 2 m; (c) the Statue of Unity and Christ the Redeemer, 144 m; (d) The Motherland Calls, 91 m.

Change the m by multiplying by 100 and add the cm that are left. Then compare the two numbers.
The tool shows both lengths in cm. Compare the two numbers: the bigger number is the longer length.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Sonu's stole is 285 cm long and Shikha's stole is 2 m 60 cm long. Which is longer, and by how much?
2. First change both to cm. 2 m 60 cm = 2 × 100 + 60 = 260 cm.
3. The difference is the longer length minus the shorter length: 285 − 260 = 25 cm.
4. So Sonu's stole is longer by 25 cm.
5. Doubling a length means multiplying it by 2. A rope of 90 cm doubled is 90 × 2 = 180 cm.
6. To find the length that becomes 180 cm when doubled, halve it: 180 ÷ 2 = 90 cm.
7. Rule: the difference is the bigger length minus the smaller length in the same unit. To undo doubling, halve.

content.text:
Worked example: Sonu's stole is 285 cm long and Shikha's stole is 2 m 60 cm long (practice values). Which is longer and by how much? A third piece doubled is 180 cm long. How long is the third piece?
1. Change 2 m 60 cm to cm: 2 × 100 + 60 = 260 cm.
2. Compare 285 and 260: 285 is more, so Sonu's stole is longer.
3. Subtract the smaller from the bigger: 285 − 260 = 25 cm.
4. A piece that doubled is 180 cm: doubling is × 2, so the piece is 180 ÷ 2 = 90 cm.
5. Check: 260 + 25 = 285 and 90 × 2 = 180.
Answer: Sonu's stole is longer by 25 cm, and the third piece is 90 cm long

media.teaching_notes: 1. Change both sides to the same unit, cm, then compare. 1 m = 100 cm. 2. (a): 5 m = 5 × 100 = 500 cm. 456 is less than 500, so 456 cm < 5 m. 3. (b): 55 cm + 200 cm = 255 cm and 200 cm + 54 cm = 254 cm. 255 is more than 254, so the left side is more. 4. (c): 6 m 5 cm = 6 × 100 + 5 = 605 cm and 6 m 50 cm = 6 × 100 + 50 = 650 cm. 605 is less than 650, so the left side is less. 5. (d): 2 m 150 cm = 2 × 100 + 150 = 350 cm and 3 m 50 cm = 3 × 100 + 50 = 350 cm. They are equal. 6. (e): 138 cm + 1 m = 138 + 100 = 238 cm. 238 cm is equal to 238 cm. 7. Check (c): 5 cm is less than 50 cm, so 6 m 5 cm is less than 6 m 50 cm. Answer: (a): <; (b): >; (c): <; (d): =; (e): =

media.teaching_notes: 1. List the heights from the tallest to the shortest: 182 m, 128 m, 108 m, 93 m, 91 m, 38 m. 2. Find the difference of each statue and the next one in the list: 182 − 128 = 54 m, 128 − 108 = 20 m, 108 − 93 = 15 m, 93 − 91 = 2 m, 91 − 38 = 53 m. 3. Two statues that are not next to each other have a statue between them, so they differ by even more. 4. The least difference is 2 m, between the Statue of Liberty (93 m) and The Motherland Calls (91 m). 5. Check: 93 − 91 = 2, and every other pair is farther apart. Answer: The Statue of Liberty and The Motherland Calls, 2 m apart

Compare them using $<$, $=$, $>$ signs. $(a)$: $456\text{ cm } \underline{\hspace{1.2em}} 5\text{ m}$; $(b)$: $55\text{ cm} + 200\text{ cm } \underline{\hspace{1.2em}} 200\text{ cm} + 54\text{ cm}$; $(c)$: $6\text{ m } 5\text{ cm } \underline{\hspace{1.2em}} 6\text{ m } 50\text{ cm}$; $(d)$: $2\text{ m } 150\text{ cm } \underline{\hspace{1.2em}} 3\text{ m } 50\text{ cm}$; $(e)$: $238\text{ cm } \underline{\hspace{1.2em}} 138\text{ cm} + 1\text{ m}$.

content.text:
1. Change both sides to the same unit, cm, then compare. $1\text{ m} = 100\text{ cm}$.
2. $(a)$: $5\text{ m} = 5 \times 100 = 500\text{ cm}$. $456$ is less than $500$, so $456\text{ cm} < 5\text{ m}$.
3. $(b)$: $55\text{ cm} + 200\text{ cm} = 255\text{ cm}$ and $200\text{ cm} + 54\text{ cm} = 254\text{ cm}$. $255$ is more than $254$, so the left side is more.
4. $(c)$: $6\text{ m } 5\text{ cm} = 6 \times 100 + 5 = 605\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ m } 50\text{ cm} = 6 \times 100 + 50 = 650\text{ cm}$. $605$ is less than $650$, so the left side is less.
5. $(d)$: $2\text{ m } 150\text{ cm} = 2 \times 100 + 150 = 350\text{ cm}$ and $3\text{ m } 50\text{ cm} = 3 \times 100 + 50 = 350\text{ cm}$. They are equal.
[Image: Let Us Compare: Ans1: solution]
6. $(e)$: $138\text{ cm} + 1\text{ m} = 138 + 100 = 238\text{ cm}$. $238\text{ cm}$ is equal to $238\text{ cm}$.
7. Check $(c)$: $5\text{ cm}$ is less than $50\text{ cm}$, so $6\text{ m } 5\text{ cm}$ is less than $6\text{ m } 50\text{ cm}$.
Answer: $(a)$: $<$; $(b)$: $>$; $(c)$: $<$; $(d)$: $=$; $(e)$: $=$
[Image: Let Us Compare: Ans1: solution (continued)]

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S6.T6.C24.IMG1}}
1. If a statue doubled is $182\text{ m}$, its height is half of $182\text{ m}$.
2. $182 \div 2 = 91\text{ m}$.
3. The Motherland Calls is $91\text{ m}$ tall.
4. Check: $91 \times 2 = 182$, and no other statue has a height that doubles to $182$.
Answer: The Motherland Calls, $91\text{ m}$

tool_config.title: Kilometre Track
tool_config.screen: The road outside the weaving centre, drawn as a long straight strip in a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, with a kilometre scale along it marked every 100 m. The track strip is the largest object on screen, 1 km long in the rope stage and 3 km long in the race stage. A rope tray holds rope pieces of a chosen length (1,000 m, 100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m, 250 m and the practice lengths), and a rope snaps end to end onto the track where the last one stopped. A stop tray holds stop markers: a water cup, a child, a red flag and a blue flag, and an interval box takes a length in m; Place stops puts a marker at every interval from the start, and a list beside the track shows the positions from the start in m and in km. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: pick a rope length and drag ropes onto the track; pick an interval and a marker and tap Place stops; Undo; type an answer into a box; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the track being worked), Reset (restores both tracks), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: ropes placed, the metres filled out of 1,000 m, the number of stops, and the list of positions.
feedback: Each rope snaps onto the track where the last rope stopped and the counter shows the metres filled, for example 4 ropes of 250 m fill 1,000 m, which is 1 km.
If the ropes run past the end of the track, the tool says: The track is only 1,000 m long. Take a rope away.
Place stops puts a marker at every interval from the start and lists the positions, and the tool says, for example: 3,000 ÷ 500 = 6, so there are 6 stops.
If the student places a stop at the start line, the tool says: Here the first stop is after the first interval, not at the start line. Try again.
A wrong count slides back with a clue such as: How many pieces of that length fit in the whole distance?

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): fill the 1 km track with ropes of 125 m. How many ropes? Answer: 8 ropes, because 1,000 ÷ 125 = 8.
Card 2 (practice values): fill the 1 km track with ropes of 50 m. How many ropes? Answer: 20 ropes, because 1,000 ÷ 50 = 20.

Card 3 (practice values): on a 2 km track place a marker after every 250 m and read the positions. Answer: 2,000 ÷ 250 = 8 markers, at 250 m, 500 m, 750 m, 1 km, 1 km 250 m, 1 km 500 m, 1 km 750 m and 2 km.

Card 4 (practice values): on the same 2 km track compare an interval of 400 m with an interval of 200 m. Answer: 5 stops for 400 m and 10 stops for 200 m, because 2,000 ÷ 400 = 5 and 2,000 ÷ 200 = 10. A smaller interval gives more stops.
Card 5: drag a marker to 1 km 500 m on the track and type its position in m. Answer: 1,500 m, because 1 × 1,000 + 500 = 1,500.
Challenge: 'Ropes of different lengths are used to make 1 km.' How many ropes of 100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m and 250 m make 1 km? Answer: 10, 100, 5, 2 and 4 ropes.

Challenge: 'Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a 3 km race.' Water stations after every 500 m: how many, and where? Children at an interval of 300 m: how many, and where? Answer: 6 water stations at 500 m, 1 km, 1 km 500 m, 2 km, 2 km 500 m and 3 km; 10 children at every 300 m from 300 m to 3,000 m; 60 flags, 30 red and 30 blue.

hint_ladder.text: How many metres are in the whole distance? Change km to m first.
How long is one piece? How many pieces of that length fill the whole distance?
Divide the whole distance in m by the length of one piece. The stops stand at 1, 2, 3 and so on times the length of one piece.
The tool fills the track piece by piece and counts them for you: the number of pieces is the answer.

content.text:
Here are some ways in which you can measure long distances.
When we walk 1,000 m, we say we have walked 1 km.
1,000 m = 1 km
Kilo stands for thousand. This unit is used to measure long distances.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many metres do you walk to cover 1 km?
2. When we walk 1,000 m, we say we have walked 1 km. So 1 km = 1,000 m.
3. Kilo stands for thousand. A km is 1,000 times as long as a m, so the km is used to measure long distances.
4. Your maths book shows four ways to measure long distances: a long tape, a rodometer (a measuring wheel), a rangefinder and a laser distance meter.
5. To change km to m, multiply by 1,000: 7 km = 7 × 1,000 = 7,000 m.
6. To change m to km, take out the thousands: 5,400 m = 5,000 m + 400 m = 5 km 400 m.
7. Rule: 1 km = 1,000 m, so multiply by 1,000 to change km to m.

content.text:
Worked example: A path is 7 km long. How many m is that? A road is 5,400 m long. How many km and m is that? (practice values)
1. 1 km = 1,000 m, so multiply the km by 1,000.
2. 7 km = 7 × 1,000 = 7,000 m.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a 2 km cycle track has a flag after every 400 m. How many flags are needed, and where do they stand?
2. First change 2 km to m: 2 km = 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 m.
3. Each piece of the track is 400 m long, so divide: 2,000 ÷ 400 = 5 pieces, and so 5 flags.
4. The flags stand at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 times 400 m from the start: 400 m, 800 m, 1,200 m, 1,600 m and 2,000 m. The last flag is at the end.
5. The same idea tells how many ropes make 1 km. If every rope is 125 m long, 1,000 ÷ 125 = 8 ropes make 1 km.
6. Rule: the number of equal pieces is the whole distance ÷ the length of one piece. The stops stand at 1, 2, 3 and so on times the length of one piece.

content.text:
1. This is an activity at your school and near your home. The numbers below are practice values that show how to do it. Yours will differ.
2. Use a long tape to measure $100\text{ m}$ and $200\text{ m}$ on the playground, mark the points and walk each line, counting steps. Practice values: $100\text{ m}$ takes $125$ steps and $200\text{ m}$ takes $250$ steps.
3. Find the length of one step: $100\text{ m} = 100 \times 100 = 10,000\text{ cm}$, and $10,000 \div 125 = 80\text{ cm}$. So one step is $80\text{ cm}$.
[Image: Measuring Long Distances: Ans1: solution]
4. Use the step to find other distances. A tea shop is $120\text{ m}$ away: $12,000 \div 80 = 150$ steps. A school gate is $400\text{ m}$ away: $40,000 \div 80 = 500$ steps. A temple is $1,600\text{ m}$ away: $160,000 \div 80 = 2,000$ steps.
5. $(a)$: The nearest is the tea shop, $120\text{ m}$. The farthest is the temple, $1,600\text{ m}$.
6. $(b)$: In increasing order: $120\text{ m}$, $400\text{ m}$, $1,600\text{ m}$.
7. $(c)$: The temple is more than $1,000\text{ m}$ away: $1,600\text{ m} = 1\text{ km } 600\text{ m}$.
8. Check: $125 \times 80 = 10,000\text{ cm}$, which is $100\text{ m}$.
Answer: Sample answer, practice values: nearest $120\text{ m}$; farthest $1,600\text{ m}$; in order $120\text{ m}$, $400\text{ m}$, $1,600\text{ m}$; $(c)$: $1\text{ km } 600\text{ m}$. Your answer may differ.
[Image: Measuring Long Distances: Ans1: solution (continued)]

content.publication_text:
1. Change $3\text{ km}$ to m: $3 \times 1,000 = 3,000\text{ m}$.
2. A flag at every $50\text{ m}$: $3,000 \div 50 = 60$ flags till the finish line. The first flag is at $50\text{ m}$ and the last is at the finish line.

4. $60 \div 2 = 30$, so there are $30$ red flags and $30$ blue flags.

content.text:
1. Find the distance of each pair from the table.
2. Guwahati is $556\text{ km}$ and Dimapur is $306\text{ km}$ from Dibrugarh: $556 - 306 = 250\text{ km}$.
3. Bhubaneswar is $2,007\text{ km}$ and Jalpaiguri Road is $983\text{ km}$ from Dibrugarh: $2,007 - 983 = 1,024\text{ km}$.
4. Compare $1,024$ and $250$: $1,024\text{ km}$ is more.
5. So Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road are farther apart.
6. Check: $306 + 250 = 556$ and $983 + 1,024 = 2,007$.
Answer: Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road: $1,024\text{ km}$, against $250\text{ km}$

tool_config.idea: Read and draw lengths in cm and mm using the small marks of a ruler: a length is the cm mark before its end plus the number of small marks after it, and 1 cm = 10 mm.
tool_config.title: Millimetre Ruler
tool_config.screen: The ruler desk of the village weaving centre, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A big yellow ruler, the largest object on screen, is marked in cm with 10 equal parts in every cm: the cm marks are long and numbered, the 5 mm marks are medium and the other marks are short, so there are 9 small marks between two cm marks. A zoom lens on a handle magnifies the centimetre it covers. A line lies on the ruler with a draggable end point that snaps to each mm mark, and objects to measure (a sprout, a small screw and a nail, with practice lengths) lie beside the ruler. A read-out shows the length in two forms, for example 4 cm 6 mm = 46 mm. The design of four nested shapes in your maths book can be placed on the desk with its eight lines, each line with a box for cm and mm. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the end of the line along the ruler; tap the lens to zoom; type into the cm box and the mm box; drag the ruler along a line of the design; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the line of this card), Reset (restores the ruler and the objects), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the length in cm and mm, the length in mm, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: The end point snaps to the nearest mm mark and the read-out says the length, for example: 4 cm and 6 small marks, 4 cm 6 mm, which is 46 mm.
If the student reads only the cm mark, the tool says: The line goes past the 4 cm mark. Count the small marks after it.
The lens makes the small marks big so that they can be counted one by one, and the counted marks light up in turn.
A wrong mm number slides back with a clue such as: Each small mark is 1 mm. Count again from the cm mark.
In the design, the ruler lays itself along the chosen line and the tool says the length only after the student has typed a reading.
tool_config.done_when: All five practice cards are solved, the small marks are counted, the eight lines of the design are measured and the five lines are drawn.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): the sprout ends on the 4th small mark after the 2 cm mark. Read its length. Answer: 2 cm 4 mm = 2 × 10 + 4 = 24 mm.
Card 2 (practice values): the screw ends on the 9th small mark after the 3 cm mark. Read its length. Answer: 3 cm 9 mm = 3 × 10 + 9 = 39 mm.
Card 3 (practice values): drag the end of a line to draw 4 cm 6 mm, then write it in mm. Answer: 4 × 10 + 6 = 46 mm.
Card 4 (practice values): drag the end of a line to draw 72 mm and write it in cm and mm. Answer: 72 mm = 70 mm + 2 mm = 7 cm 2 mm.
Card 5 (practice values): a nail is 2 cm 8 mm long and a bead is 25 mm long. Which is longer, and by how much? Answer: 2 cm 8 mm = 28 mm and 28 − 25 = 3 mm, so the nail is longer by 3 mm.

Then: 'Measure the lines in the design and write their measurements in cm and mm.' A ruler may read 1 mm different.

topics.summary: One centimetre is divided into ten equal parts of 1 mm, so 1 cm = 10 mm. A length in cm and mm is written in mm by multiplying the cm by 10 and adding the mm.

content.text:
One centimetre is divided into ten equal parts. Each part is called 1 millimetre (mm).
1 cm = 10 mm
These small marks between any two centimetre marks help us measure the smaller lengths. Thus, it adds to the precision in measurement.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a sprout, a small screw and a nail are shorter than most things you measure. How can you measure them? How many small marks are there between 1 cm and 2 cm on a ruler?
2. Look at a ruler. Between any two centimetre marks there are 9 small marks. They cut 1 cm into 10 equal parts.
3. Each part is called 1 millimetre, written 1 mm. So 1 cm = 10 mm.
4. The small marks help us measure smaller lengths and give a more exact measurement. A sprout, a small screw or a nail can be measured with them.
5. To change cm to mm, multiply by 10: 3 cm = 3 × 10 = 30 mm.
6. A length of 8 mm is less than 1 cm, because 8 is less than 10.
7. Rule: 1 cm = 10 mm, so multiply by 10 to change cm to mm.

1. 1 cm = 10 mm, so multiply the cm by 10.
2. 3 cm = 3 × 10 = 30 mm.
3. 1 cm = 10 mm, and 8 is less than 10.
4. So 8 mm is less than 1 cm.
5. Check: 30 mm is 3 groups of 10 mm, which is 3 cm.
Answer: 3 cm = 30 mm, and 8 mm is less than 1 cm

content.text:
1. Predict first: a line starts at 0 and ends on the 6th small mark after the 4 cm mark. How long is it?
2. Read the cm first: 4 cm. Then count the small marks after it: 6 small marks are 6 mm. The length is 4 cm 6 mm.
3. To write it in mm, change the cm to mm and add the rest: 4 cm 6 mm = 4 × 10 + 6 = 46 mm.
4. To draw a length given in mm, split it into tens and ones. 72 mm is 70 mm + 2 mm = 7 cm 2 mm. Put the 0 of the scale at the start, go to the 7 cm mark, then 2 small marks more.
5. The same works for any length in mm. 52 mm is 5 cm 2 mm: go to the 5 cm mark and then 2 small marks more. The tens of mm are cm and the ones are the small marks.
6. Rule: the tens of mm are cm and the ones are mm, so 46 mm is 4 cm 6 mm.

content.text:
Worked example: A line ends on the 6th small mark after the 4 cm mark. Write its length in cm and mm and in mm only. Then say how to draw a line of 72 mm (practice values).
1. The line passes the 4 cm mark and ends 6 small marks later. 6 small marks are 6 mm.
2. The length is 4 cm 6 mm.
3. In mm: 4 cm = 4 × 10 = 40 mm, and 40 + 6 = 46 mm.
4. To draw 72 mm, split 72 into tens and ones: 72 = 70 + 2.
5. 70 mm is 7 cm, so 72 mm = 7 cm 2 mm.
6. Put the 0 of the scale at the start of the line, go to the 7 cm mark, then 2 small marks more, and mark the end.
7. Check: 7 × 10 + 2 = 72 mm.
Answer: 4 cm 6 mm = 46 mm, and a line of 72 mm is drawn to 7 cm 2 mm

In mm that is 5 × 10 + 5 = 55 mm. 3. (b): 3 cm 6 mm: go to 3 cm and then 6 small marks. In mm that is 3 × 10 + 6 = 36 mm. 4. (c): 8 cm 3 mm: go to 8 cm and then 3 small marks. 4. The sprout grows, so each day's length should be more than the day before: $3 < 9 < 16 < 25$.

3. $(b)$: $3\text{ cm } 6\text{ mm}$: go to $3\text{ cm}$ and then $6$ small marks. In mm that is $3 \times 10 + 6 = 36\text{ mm}$.

tool_config.idea: Change a length from one unit to another with the multipliers 10, 100 and 1,000 on two linked number lines, and split a length into a part in the bigger unit and a rest in the smaller unit.
tool_config.title: Double Number Line
tool_config.screen: A pair of tapes on the weaving centre wall, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: the top tape in the bigger unit and the bottom tape in the smaller unit, with their ticks lined up one under the other. The two lines are the largest object on screen. A draggable pointer moves along both tapes together, so one tick shows the same length in two units. A unit switch picks cm over mm, m over cm or km over m. Multiplier boxes sit on the arrows between the tapes (for example ×10 from the top tape down to the bottom tape) and take a number. Tick labels may be blank for the student to fill in. Under the tapes a split tray cuts a length such as 5,792 cm into a part that is whole metres (5,700 cm) and a rest (92 cm), and joins them as 57 m 92 cm. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the pointer; tap a blank label and type a number; tap a multiplier box and type; drag the split mark in the tray; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the blanks of this card), Reset (restores the lines), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the same length on both tapes, the multiplier used, the split parts, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: The pointer moves on both tapes at once and the read-out shows both numbers with their units and the multiplier, for example: 6 cm is 6 × 10 = 60 mm.
A blank label accepts only the number that belongs to that tick. A wrong number slides back with a clue such as: Going down the multiplier is 10, so multiply the top number by 10.
A multiplier box is checked against the two numbers above and below it, and the tool says, for example: ×10 is right because 7 × 10 = 70.
In the split tray the part in the bigger unit and the rest are shown in two colours, and the tool says: 5,700 cm is 57 m, and 92 cm are left, so 57 m 92 cm.
In the conversion tasks the tool says whether the answer is right and gives a clue; it never fills the answer in before the third hint.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many mm are in 6 cm? How many cm are in 9 m? How many m are in 8 km?

5. Going up from the bottom line to the top line, divide by the same number: 4,000 m = 4,000 ÷ 1,000 = 4 km.
6. Rule: from a bigger unit to a smaller unit multiply by 10, 100 or 1,000, and from a smaller unit to a bigger unit divide.

1. Going from a bigger unit to a smaller unit, multiply.

2. Change the metres: 7,300 ÷ 100 = 73, so 7,300 cm = 73 m.
3. So 7,305 cm = 73 m 5 cm.
4. Now 3 m 7 cm: 3 m = 3 × 100 = 300 cm.
5. 300 cm + 7 cm = 307 cm, so 3 m 7 cm = 307 cm.
6. Check: 73 × 100 + 5 = 7,305.
Answer: 7,305 cm = 73 m 5 cm and 3 m 7 cm = 307 cm

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S15.T15.C65.IMG1}}
1. The top line is in cm and the bottom line is in mm. Going down, multiply by $10$, because $1\text{ cm} = 10\text{ mm}$.
2. The arrow $\times 7$ on the top line goes from $1\text{ cm}$ to $7\text{ cm}$, so the arrow on the bottom line from $10\text{ mm}$ to the next blank is also $\times 7$: $10 \times 7 = 70\text{ mm}$.
3. $7\text{ cm} = 7 \times 10 = 70\text{ mm}$, and the box on the arrow from the top line to the bottom line is $\times 10$. $15\text{ cm} = 15 \times 10 = 150\text{ mm}$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
4. Going up, divide by $10$: $250 \div 10 = 25\text{ cm}$, $320 \div 10 = 32\text{ cm}$ and $450 \div 10 = 45\text{ cm}$.
5. $50\text{ cm} = 50 \times 10 = 500\text{ mm}$. Your maths book prints m under this tick, but $50\text{ cm}$ is $500\text{ mm}$, which is also half a metre.
6. Check: $7 \times 10 = 70$ and $70 \div 10 = 7$.
Answer: Top: $25\text{ cm}$, $32\text{ cm}$, $45\text{ cm}$. Bottom: $70\text{ mm}$, $150\text{ mm}$, $500\text{ mm}$. Boxes: $\times 7$, $\times 10$
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

tool_config.idea: Add and subtract lengths given in two units in a column for each unit, with exchange chips for regrouping: 1 km = 1,000 m and 1 m = 100 cm.
tool_config.title: Length Columns
tool_config.screen: The cutting table of the village weaving centre, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, with a chart of two columns on the wall. The chart is the largest object on screen: columns headed km and m (or m and cm), rows for the first length, the second length and the answer, and a plus or minus sign on the left. Number tiles sit in the cells. Exchange chips wait beside the chart: a chip marked 1 km turns into 1,000 m and back, and a chip marked 1 m turns into 100 cm and back. A check strip below changes the whole sum to the smaller unit as a second way. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a cell and type a number; drag an exchange chip across a column border; tap Add or Subtract; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the cells of this card), Reset (restores the table), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the sum in the smaller unit, the carried or exchanged amount, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: Typing in a cell shows the number in its column. If a cell holds more than a full bigger unit, the tool says, for example: 1,700 m is more than 1,000 m, so exchange 1,000 m for 1 km.
An exchange chip moves across the column border and the numbers change together, for example 1 km becomes 1,000 m.
In a subtraction, if the bottom number is bigger than the top number in a column, the tool says: You cannot take 40 cm from 0 cm. Exchange 1 m for 100 cm first.
The check strip changes the whole sum to the smaller unit and shows that both ways give the same length.
A wrong answer slides back with a clue such as: Did you exchange 1 m as 100 cm and not as 10 cm?
tool_config.done_when: All five practice cards are solved, the two examples are worked, and the three word problems and the seven pairs are answered.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): add 2 km 900 m and 1 km 800 m in the km and m columns. Answer: 900 m + 800 m = 1,700 m, carry 1 km and write 700 m, and 2 km + 1 km + 1 km = 4 km, so 4 km 700 m.
Card 2 (practice values): add 5 m 60 cm and 3 m 70 cm in the m and cm columns. Answer: 60 cm + 70 cm = 130 cm, carry 1 m and write 30 cm, and 5 m + 3 m + 1 m = 9 m, so 9 m 30 cm.
Card 3 (practice values): subtract 3 m 40 cm from 9 m. Answer: exchange 1 m for 100 cm, so 9 m becomes 8 m 100 cm, and 8 m 100 cm − 3 m 40 cm = 5 m 60 cm.
Card 4 (practice values): subtract 2 km 600 m from 5 km 200 m. Answer: exchange 1 km for 1,000 m, so 5 km 200 m becomes 4 km 1,200 m, and 4 km 1,200 m − 2 km 600 m = 2 km 600 m.
Card 5: check card 4 by changing to m. Answer: 5,200 − 2,600 = 2,600 m = 2 km 600 m.

Challenge: 'Saji saw on his smartphone that he walked 3 km 450 m in the morning and another 4 km 650 m in the evening. How much did he walk in the whole day?' and 'They need 63 m of cable for this purpose. They used 16 m 75 cm cable in the first room. What is the length of the cable left?' Answer: 8 km 100 m, and 46 m 25 cm.

Challenge: 'Rani has two red coloured ribbon rolls, one of length 3 m 75 cm and another 2 m 25 cm long. How much ribbon does she have?'; 'The distance from Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m ... 17 km 900 m away from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?'; 'The first section covers 2 km 300 m and the second section covers 2 km 650 m'; and 'Circle the bigger length and find the difference' for the seven pairs. Answer: 6 m; 30 km 800 m; 4 km 950 m; and the pairs: (a) 11 mm, 1 mm; (b) 26 mm, 6 mm; (c) 201 mm, 1 mm; (d) 1,020 mm, 20 mm; (e) 245 cm, 45 cm; (f) 6 km, 322 m; (g) 6 km 1,480 m, 1 m.

content.publication_text: Electricians are changing the cables in a house. They need $63\text{ m}$ of cable for this purpose. They used $16\text{ m } 75\text{ cm}$ cable in the first room. What is the length of the cable left?

content.text:
1. The two lengths are in m and cm. Change both to cm: $1\text{ m} = 100\text{ cm}$.
2. $63\text{ m} = 63 \times 100 = 6,300\text{ cm}$ and $16\text{ m } 75\text{ cm} = 16 \times 100 + 75 = 1,675\text{ cm}$.
3. Subtract: $6,300 - 1,675 = 4,625\text{ cm}$.
4. Change back: $4,625\text{ cm} = 4,600\text{ cm} + 25\text{ cm} = 46\text{ m } 25\text{ cm}$.

content.publication_text: Circle the bigger length and find the difference. $(e)$: $2\text{ m}$ and $245\text{ cm}$; $(f)$: $5,678\text{ m}$ and $6\text{ km}$; $(g)$: $6\text{ km } 1,480\text{ m}$ and $7\text{ km } 479\text{ m}$.

content.text:
1. Change both lengths to the smaller unit, then compare and subtract.
2. $(e)$: $2\text{ m} = 200\text{ cm}$. $245\text{ cm}$ is more than $200\text{ cm}$. The difference is $245 - 200 = 45\text{ cm}$.
3. $(f)$: $6\text{ km} = 6,000\text{ m}$. $6,000\text{ m}$ is more than $5,678\text{ m}$. The difference is $6,000 - 5,678 = 322\text{ m}$.
4. $(g)$: $6\text{ km } 1,480\text{ m} = 6,000 + 1,480 = 7,480\text{ m}$ and $7\text{ km } 479\text{ m} = 7,000 + 479 = 7,479\text{ m}$. $7,480\text{ m}$ is more than $7,479\text{ m}$, so $6\text{ km } 1,480\text{ m}$ is the bigger length. The difference is $7,480 - 7,479 = 1\text{ m}$.
5. Check: $5,678 + 322 = 6,000$.
Answer: Bigger, difference: $(e)$: $245\text{ cm}$, $45\text{ cm}$; $(f)$: $6\text{ km}$, $322\text{ m}$; $(g)$: $6\text{ km } 1,480\text{ m}$, $1\text{ m}$

tool_config.idea: Multiply and divide a length given in two units by working on each unit and then regrouping: copies of a length laid end to end give so many m and so many cm, and a road shared into equal days gives each day its km and m.
tool_config.title: Cut and Share
tool_config.screen: The cutting table of the village weaving centre with a roll of cloth and a road strip beside it, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A strip of cloth of a chosen length in m and cm lies on a tape, and it is the largest object on screen. A Make copies stepper lays copies of the strip end to end along the tape, and two piles collect the parts: a m pile and a cm pile. An exchange chip turns 100 cm into 1 m. For division, a road bar of a chosen length in km and m has a Share into stepper that fills equal day boxes, each with a km part and a m part, and a leftover chip turns 1 km into 1,000 m when the km do not share equally. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: the Make copies stepper; drag the parts of a strip into the m pile and the cm pile; tap the exchange chip; the Share into stepper; type an answer into a box; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the piles of this card), Reset (restores the roll and the road), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the number of copies, the m pile and the cm pile, the total after the exchange, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: Each copy lands at the end of the last one along the tape, and the piles count the parts: for example 5 copies give 15 m in the m pile and 100 cm in the cm pile.
When the cm pile reaches 100 cm or more, the tool says: 100 cm make 1 m. Tap the chip to change them.
For a road, each day box shows its km and its m. If the km do not share equally, the tool says: Change the whole road to m first, then share.
A wrong total slides back with a clue such as: Did you multiply the cm as well as the m?
After the exchange the tool shows the total in one line, for example 16 m, and checks it against the same length in cm.
tool_config.done_when: All five practice cards are solved, and the shirts, Anita's thread and its cost, and the road are answered.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): lay 5 copies of a strip of 3 m 20 cm and sort the parts. Answer: 5 × 3 m = 15 m and 5 × 20 cm = 100 cm = 1 m, so 16 m.
Card 2 (practice values): lay 6 copies of a strip of 1 m 50 cm and sort the parts. Answer: 6 × 1 m = 6 m and 6 × 50 cm = 300 cm = 3 m, so 9 m.
Card 3 (practice values): lay 8 copies of a strip of 2 m 25 cm and sort the parts. Answer: 8 × 2 m = 16 m and 8 × 25 cm = 200 cm = 2 m, so 18 m.
Card 4 (practice values): share a road of 24 km 800 m into 4 equal days. Answer: 24 km divided by 4 is 6 km and 800 m divided by 4 is 200 m, so 6 km 200 m a day.
Card 5 (practice values): share a road of 7 km 200 m into 4 equal days. 7 km does not share equally among 4, so change the whole road to m. Answer: 7,200 ÷ 4 = 1,800 m = 1 km 800 m a day.

Challenge: 'We need a 1 m 80 cm cloth to make a shirt for a 10 year old child. How much cloth will be needed to make shirts for 20 such children?' Then: 'Anita is making an embroidery on the border of a sari. She needs a 1 m long thread to embroider a 50 cm sari. How much thread would she need for a 5 m sari border? A 1 m long thread costs ₹50. How much money will be needed to buy the thread?' Answer: 20 × 1 m = 20 m and 20 × 80 cm = 1,600 cm = 16 m, so 36 m; the 5 m border is 500 cm and 500 ÷ 50 = 10, so 10 m of thread, and 10 × 50 = ₹500.

Challenge: 'A road 12 km 600 m long is being laid in a town. The workers lay an equal length of road each day, and complete the work in 6 days. How much road laying work is done on each day?' Answer: 12 km divided by 6 is 2 km and 600 m divided by 6 is 100 m, so 2 km 100 m a day.

hint_ladder.text: How many copies or how many days? What are the two parts of the length?
Multiply the m part and the cm part separately, or share the km part and the m part separately.
If the cm pile has 100 or more, change 100 cm to 1 m. If the km do not share equally, change the road to m.
The tool lays the pieces or shares the road and shows each pile: read the total.

student_does: Look at the video's picture of curtain strips of 2 m 40 cm laid end to end. Say which two parts you will multiply, the m and the cm, then press Next.
Lay copies of a strip end to end, sort the m and the cm into their piles, exchange 100 cm for 1 m, and share a road into equal days with a km part and a m part.
Answer your maths book's own questions: the shirts for 20 children, Anita's thread and its cost, and the road laid in 6 equal days.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: Rani sews curtains and each curtain needs 2 m 40 cm of cloth. How much cloth do 12 curtains need? Break the length into m and cm: 2 m 40 cm is 2 m and 40 cm. Multiply each part by 12. 12 × 2 m = 24 m. 12 × 40 cm = 480 cm. 480 cm is more than 100 cm, so change it to m and cm: 480 cm = 4 m 80 cm. Add the parts: 24 m + 4 m 80 cm = 28 m 80 cm. You can also change the length to cm first and multiply: 12 × 240 = 2,880 cm = 28 m 80 cm. Rule: break the length into m and cm and multiply each part, or change it to cm and multiply, and then regroup. 1. Break 2 m 40 cm into 2 m and 40 cm and multiply each part by 12. 2. 12 × 2 m = 24 m. 3. 12 × 40 cm = 480 cm. 4. 480 cm = 400 cm + 80 cm = 4 m 80 cm. 5. Add: 24 m + 4 m 80 cm = 28 m 80 cm. 6. Check in cm: 12 × 240 = 2,880 cm = 28 m 80 cm. Answer: 28 m 80 cm

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: 3 m of ribbon costs ₹90. How much does 1 m cost? How much do 9 m cost? Share the price equally among the metres: 90 ÷ 3 = ₹30 for 1 m. A double number line shows both: the top line is metres and the bottom line is rupees. If you multiply the metres by 3, multiply the price by 3 too: 3 m is ₹90, so 9 m is ₹270. To find the length for a given cost, divide the cost by the price of 1 m: ₹300 buys 300 ÷ 30 = 10 m. Rule: the price of 1 m is the price ÷ the number of metres. Then multiply it by any length. 1. Share the ₹90 equally among the 3 m: 90 ÷ 3 = ₹30 for 1 m. 2. 9 m is 3 times 3 m, so the price is 3 times ₹90: 3 × 90 = ₹270. 3. Or 9 m at ₹30 for each metre: 9 × 30 = ₹270. 4. For ₹300, divide by the price of 1 m: 300 ÷ 30 = 10 m. 5. Check: 10 × 30 = ₹300. Answer: 1 m costs ₹30, 9 m cost ₹270, and ₹300 buys 10 m

1. Predict first: Rani sews curtains and each curtain needs 2 m 40 cm of cloth. How much cloth do 12 curtains need?
2. Break the length into m and cm: 2 m 40 cm is 2 m and 40 cm. Multiply each part by 12.
3. 12 × 2 m = 24 m. 12 × 40 cm = 480 cm.
4. 480 cm is more than 100 cm, so change it to m and cm: 480 cm = 4 m 80 cm.
5. Add the parts: 24 m + 4 m 80 cm = 28 m 80 cm.
6. You can also change the length to cm first and multiply: 12 × 240 = 2,880 cm = 28 m 80 cm.
7. Rule: break the length into m and cm and multiply each part, or change it to cm and multiply, and then regroup.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a pipe line of 18 km 900 m is laid in 3 equal days. How much is laid each day?
2. Break the length into km and m: 18 km and 900 m. Divide each part by 3.
3. 18 km divided by 3 is 6 km. 900 m divided by 3 is 300 m. So each day 6 km 300 m is laid.
4. You can also change to m first: 18 km 900 m = 18,900 m, and 18,900 ÷ 3 = 6,300 m = 6 km 300 m.
5. Check by multiplying: 3 × 6 km 300 m = 18 km 900 m.
6. Rule: divide each unit part, or change to the smaller unit and divide, and then change back.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 3 m of ribbon costs ₹90. How much does 1 m cost? How much do 9 m cost?
2. Share the price equally among the metres: 90 ÷ 3 = ₹30 for 1 m.
3. A double number line shows both: the top line is metres and the bottom line is rupees. If you multiply the metres by 3, multiply the price by 3 too: 3 m is ₹90, so 9 m is ₹270.
4. To find the length for a given cost, divide the cost by the price of 1 m: ₹300 buys 300 ÷ 30 = 10 m.
5. Rule: the price of 1 m is the price ÷ the number of metres. Then multiply it by any length.

content.text:
Worked example: A shop sells ribbon at ₹90 for 3 m (practice values). What does 1 m cost? What do 9 m cost? How many m can you buy for ₹300?
1. Share the ₹90 equally among the 3 m: 90 ÷ 3 = ₹30 for 1 m.
2. 9 m is 3 times 3 m, so the price is 3 times ₹90: 3 × 90 = ₹270.
3. Or 9 m at ₹30 for each metre: 9 × 30 = ₹270.
4. For ₹300, divide by the price of 1 m: 300 ÷ 30 = 10 m.
5. Check: 10 × 30 = ₹300.
Answer: 1 m costs ₹30, 9 m cost ₹270, and ₹300 buys 10 m

content.publication_text: We need a $1\text{ m } 80\text{ cm}$ cloth to make a shirt for a $10$ year old child. How much cloth will be needed to make shirts for $20$ such children?

content.text:
1. Break the length into m and cm: $1\text{ m } 80\text{ cm}$ is $1\text{ m}$ and $80\text{ cm}$. Multiply each part by $20$.
2. $20 \times 1\text{ m} = 20\text{ m}$.
3. $20 \times 80\text{ cm} = 1,600\text{ cm}$.
4. $1,600\text{ cm} = 16\text{ m}$, because $1,600 \div 100 = 16$.
5. Add: $20\text{ m} + 16\text{ m} = 36\text{ m}$.
6. Check in cm: $20 \times 180 = 3,600\text{ cm} = 36\text{ m}$.
Answer: $36\text{ m}$

content.text:
1. The thread is $1\text{ m}$ for every $50\text{ cm}$ of the sari border. First change the $5\text{ m}$ border to cm: $5 \times 100 = 500\text{ cm}$.
2. How many pieces of $50\text{ cm}$ are in $500\text{ cm}$? $500 \div 50 = 10$.
3. Each $50\text{ cm}$ of border needs $1\text{ m}$ of thread, so $10 \times 1\text{ m} = 10\text{ m}$ of thread.
4. The thread costs ₹$50$ for $1\text{ m}$, so $10\text{ m}$ cost $10 \times 50 =$ ₹$500$.
5. Check: $10\text{ m}$ of thread for $500\text{ cm}$ of border, and $10 \times 50 = 500$.
Answer: $10\text{ m}$ of thread, costing ₹$500$

content.book_number: Multiplying and Dividing Lengths: the road
content.question_tex: A road $12\text{ km } 600\text{ m}$ long is being laid in a town. The workers lay an equal length of road each day, and complete the work in $6$ days. How much road laying work is done on each day?
content.publication_text: A road $12\text{ km } 600\text{ m}$ long is being laid in a town. The workers lay an equal length of road each day, and complete the work in $6$ days. How much road laying work is done on each day?

content.text:
1. Change the road to m: $12\text{ km } 600\text{ m} = 12 \times 1,000 + 600 = 12,600\text{ m}$.
2. The same length is laid each day for $6$ days: $12,600 \div 6 = 2,100\text{ m}$.
3. Change back: $2,100\text{ m} = 2,000\text{ m} + 100\text{ m} = 2\text{ km } 100\text{ m}$.
4. Another way: $12\text{ km}$ divided by $6$ is $2\text{ km}$, and $600\text{ m}$ divided by $6$ is $100\text{ m}$.
5. Check: $6 \times 2,100 = 12,600\text{ m}$.
Answer: $2\text{ km } 100\text{ m}$ each day

1. This depends on your own neighbourhood. The numbers below are practice values that show the method. Yours will differ.
2. Choose a reference: one floor of the building, which is about $3\text{ m}$ high (practice value).

5. The tallest building is about $15\text{ m}$ high, using one floor as the reference.
6. Check: $5$ floors on top of each other, each about $3\text{ m}$, reach about $15\text{ m}$.

content.text:
1. This depends on your own neighbourhood. The numbers below are practice values that show the method. Yours will differ.
2. Choose a reference: a friend who is $1\text{ m } 50\text{ cm}$ tall, standing beside the tallest tree.
3. Count how many friends would stand one on top of the other to reach the top of the tree: about $8$.
4. Change the reference to cm: $1\text{ m } 50\text{ cm} = 150\text{ cm}$. Multiply: $8 \times 150 = 1,200\text{ cm}$.
5. $1,200\text{ cm} = 12\text{ m}$, because $1,200 \div 100 = 12$.
6. The tallest tree is about $12\text{ m}$ high, using a friend as the reference.
Answer: Sample answer, practice values: about $12\text{ m}$, with a friend of $1\text{ m } 50\text{ cm}$ as the reference. Your answer may differ.

content.text:
Worked example: Shikha's height is 4 feet 6 inches (practice values). How many inches is that? Then change 30 inches into feet and inches.
1. 1 foot = 12 inches, so multiply the feet by 12.
2. 4 feet = 4 × 12 = 48 inches.
3. Add the 6 inches: 48 + 6 = 54 inches.
4. Now 30 inches: take out the full feet. 2 feet = 2 × 12 = 24 inches.
5. 30 − 24 = 6 inches are left, so 30 inches = 2 feet 6 inches.
6. Check: 2 × 12 + 6 = 30.
Answer: 4 feet 6 inches = 54 inches, and 30 inches = 2 feet 6 inches

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S25.T25.C118.IMG1}}
1. Look at your ruler. One edge has cm and mm marks, and the other edge may have inch marks.
2. Put the $0$ of the inch scale next to the $0$ of the cm scale. The $1$ inch mark falls $2\text{ cm}$ and $5$ small marks after $0$.
3. So $1$ inch $= 2\text{ cm } 5\text{ mm}$.
4. In mm, $2\text{ cm } 5\text{ mm} = 2 \times 10 + 5 = 25\text{ mm}$.
5. Check: $12$ inches $= 12 \times 25 = 300\text{ mm} = 30\text{ cm}$, which is $1$ foot.
Answer: $1$ inch $= 2\text{ cm } 5\text{ mm}$

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a 3 by 3 grid must have each of the signs +, − and × once in every row and once in every column. The top left box is +, the middle box is × and the bottom right box is −. Can you fill the rest? Start with a box that has only one choice. The top middle box: its row already has + and its column already has ×. So it must be −. Now the top row has +, − and ×, so the top right box is ×. The left box of the middle row: its column has + and its row has ×. So it must be −. Then the right box of the middle row is +. The bottom row: its left box must be × and its middle box must be +, with − on the right. Check every row and every column: each has +, − and × once. Rule: find the box with only one choice left, fill it, and keep using the row and the column. 1. Look for a box with only one choice. The left box of the middle row: its column has + and its row has ×, so it must be −. 4. The right box of the middle row: its row has − and ×, so it must be +. 5. The bottom left box: its column has + and −, so it must be ×. 6. The bottom middle box: its row has × and −, so it must be +. 7. Check: row 1 is +, −, ×, row 2 is −, ×, +, row 3 is ×, +, −, and each column has +, − and × once. Answer: Row 1: +, −, ×; row 2: −, ×, +; row 3: ×, +, −

3. Now the top row has +, − and ×, so the top right box is ×.

5. The bottom row: its left box must be × and its middle box must be +, with − on the right.
6. Check every row and every column: each has +, − and × once.
7. Rule: find the box with only one choice left, fill it, and keep using the row and the column.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S28.T28.C124.IMG1}}
1. Each row, each column and each $2 \times 2$ box has $+$, $-$, $\times$ and $\div$ once. Start with a box that has only one choice.
2. Row $1$ has $\div$ and $+$, so its other two boxes are $-$ and $\times$ . Column $2$ already has $\times$ in row $2$, so the top second box is $-$ and the top third box is $\times$ .
[Image: Try This: Ans1: solution]
3. Row $4$ needs $\div$ , $+$ and $\times$ in its first three boxes. Column $3$ already has $\times$ and $+$, so the bottom third box is $\div$ . Column $2$ already has $-$ and $\times$ , so the bottom second box is $+$, and the bottom first box is $\times$ .
4. Row $2$ needs $\div$ , $+$ and $-$ in its other boxes. Column $4$ already has $+$ and $-$, so the right box of row $2$ is $\div$ . Column $3$ already has $\times$ , $+$ and $\div$ , so the third box of row $2$ is $-$, and the first box is $+$.
5. Row $3$ needs $-$, $\div$ and $\times$ . Column $1$ already has $\div$ , $+$ and $\times$ , so the first box of row $3$ is $-$. Column $2$ already has $-$, $\times$ and $+$, so the second box is $\div$ , and the last box is $\times$ .
6. The completed grid: row $1 \div$ , $-$, $\times$ , $+$; row $2 +$, $\times$ , $-$, $\div$ ; row $3 -$, $\div$ , $+$, $\times$ ; row $4 \times$ , $+$, $\div$ , $-$.
7. Check: every row, every column and every $2 \times 2$ box has all four signs once.
Answer: Row $1$: $\div$ , $-$, $\times$ , $+$; row $2$: $+$, $\times$ , $-$, $\div$ ; row $3$: $-$, $\div$ , $+$, $\times$ ; row $4$: $\times$ , $+$, $\div$ , $-$
[Image: Try This: Ans1: solution (continued)]

topics.summary: The chapter's ideas in one walk along the measuring tape: the unit that fits, one length in two units, comparing and the difference, the kilometre and equal pieces, distance between stations, the millimetre, changing units, adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing lengths, the price of a length, estimating, feet and inches, and the sign puzzle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have walked along the whole measuring tape of the weaving centre. Can you say one idea from each stop, from the unit that fits to the sign puzzle? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Choosing a unit: short things such as a pencil are measured in cm and long things such as a wall are measured in m, so the number sounds sensible.
3. One length, two names: 1 m = 100 cm. 3 m = 3 × 100 = 300 cm, and 450 cm = 4 m 50 cm.
4. Check: 5 m = 5 × 100 = 500 cm, so 480 cm is less than 5 m.
5. Comparing: change both lengths to the same unit, then compare. 4 m 3 cm = 403 cm, which is less than 430 cm.
6. Difference: the bigger length minus the smaller length in the same unit. 285 − 260 = 25 cm.
7. The kilometre: 1 km = 1,000 m, so 7 km = 7 × 1,000 = 7,000 m.
8. Equal pieces: a 2 km track with a flag after every 400 m needs 2,000 ÷ 400 = 5 flags.
9. Check: how many ropes of 125 m make 1 km? 1,000 ÷ 125 = 8 ropes.
10. Distance between two stations: subtract the two distances from the start. 615 − 340 = 275 km.
11. The millimetre: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 3 cm = 3 × 10 = 30 mm, and 4 cm 6 mm = 4 × 10 + 6 = 46 mm.
12. Changing units: from a bigger unit to a smaller unit multiply by 10, 100 or 1,000, and from a smaller unit to a bigger unit divide. 9 m = 9 × 100 = 900 cm and 4,000 m = 4,000 ÷ 1,000 = 4 km.
13. Check: write 7,305 cm in m and cm. 7,305 cm = 7,300 cm + 5 cm = 73 m 5 cm.
14. Adding: add like units and regroup. 2 km 700 m + 1 km 800 m = 4 km 500 m.
15. Subtracting: change both to the smaller unit, or regroup 1 m as 100 cm. 9 m − 3 m 40 cm = 5 m 60 cm.
16. Multiplying and dividing: break the length into two units and work on each. 12 × 2 m 40 cm = 28 m 80 cm, and 18 km 900 m divided by 3 is 6 km 300 m.
17. Price: 3 m of ribbon costs ₹90, so 1 m costs 90 ÷ 3 = ₹30.
18. Estimating: pick a reference you know, count how many times it fits, and say about. A wall as high as 2 doors of 2 m is about 4 m high.
19. Feet and inches: 1 foot = 12 inches. 4 feet 6 inches = 4 × 12 + 6 = 54 inches.
20. Sign puzzle: fill the box that has only one choice left, using its row and its column.

objectives.objective_text: Students choose cm or m for a length by asking how big the thing is and picking the unit that gives a sensible number.
Students change a length from m to cm and from cm to m and cm using 1 m = 100 cm.
Students choose the unit, m or cm, for six lengths, and name the same length in m and cm by filling in number lines side by side and matching lengths.
Students compare two lengths given in different units by changing both to the same unit and then comparing the numbers.
Students find how much longer one length is than another by changing both to one unit and subtracting, and find the length that doubles to a given length.

Students compare the length of rods with <, = and > by changing to one unit, and find the difference of two statue heights, the least and the largest differences, and the statue that doubles to the tallest.

objectives.objective_text: Students explain that 1 cm is divided into 10 equal parts called millimetres, count the small marks, and change cm to mm using 1 cm = 10 mm.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students read a length from a ruler in cm and mm and in mm only, and draw a line of a given length.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students count the small marks between two cm marks on a ruler, measure the lines of a design in cm and mm, record the length of a sprout in mm, and draw lines of given lengths.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students change lengths between mm and cm, cm and m, and m and km by multiplying or dividing by 10, 100 or 1,000.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students write a length in one unit as a length in two units, and a length in two units as one number in the smaller unit, by splitting it.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students fill in the numbers and the multipliers on three number lines side by side, and change lengths between mm, cm, m and km in fourteen conversions.
Students add two lengths given in two units by adding like units, or by changing both to the smaller unit and adding.
Students subtract one length from another by changing both to the smaller unit or by regrouping a bigger unit into the smaller one.
Students add and subtract lengths given in two units in the book's examples and word problems, and find the bigger of two lengths and their difference.
Students multiply a length given in m and cm by a whole number by multiplying the m and the cm separately and regrouping.
Students divide a length given in km and m by a whole number by dividing each unit part, or by changing it to the smaller unit.
Students find the price of 1 m from the price of a longer piece and use it to find the cost of a given length and the length for a given cost.
Students find the cloth for many shirts, the price of 1 m, the thread and its cost for a border, and share a road into equal days to find the length laid each day.
Students estimate a height or a depth by choosing a reference length and counting how many times it fits.
Students estimate the height of a building, the height of a tree and the depth of a well or pool, and say which reference length they used.
Students change a height between feet and inches and inches using 1 foot = 12 inches, and say that 1 inch is 2 cm 5 mm.
Students find how many cm and mm make 1 inch, and write the heights of students in feet and inches and find the tallest.
Students fill a small grid with three signs so that no sign repeats in a row or a column, using the clues one at a time.
Students fill the book's 4 by 4 grid with the signs +, −, × and ÷ so that no sign repeats in any row, column or 2 × 2 box.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Identify the appropriate units for measuring each of the following. Write m or cm after each number. (a): the height of India Gate is 42 ___; (b): the length of a handkerchief is 40 ___; (c): the depth of a well is 50 ___; (d): the length of a mobile phone is 13 ___; (e): the length of an elephant's trunk is 2 ___; (f): the distance between two buttons on a shirt is 5 ___.

Book item: Shikha and Sonu are measuring the lengths of saris and stoles in the village weaving centre. You can take help of the double number line below. Fill in the blanks. Top line: 100 cm, ___ cm, 400 cm, 500 cm, 700 cm. Bottom line: 1 m, 2 m, ___ m, ___ m, ___ m.

Book item: Shikha and Sonu are measuring the lengths of saris and stoles in the village weaving centre. Find which measures represent the same sari or stole. First list: 204 cm, 540 cm, 750 cm, 240 cm, 404 cm. Second list: 5 m 40 cm, 2 m 204 cm, 2 m 4 cm, 2 m 40 cm, 6 m 150 cm.

Book item: Ritika is comparing the lengths of different rods. Compare them using <, =, > signs. (a): 456 cm ___ 5 m; (b): 55 cm + 200 cm ___ 200 cm + 54 cm; (c): 6 m 5 cm ___ 6 m 50 cm; (d): 2 m 150 cm ___ 3 m 50 cm; (e): 238 cm ___ 138 cm + 1 m.
Book item: Look at the picture of some of the world's tallest statues. What is the difference between the height of the tallest statue in the world and the Statue of Liberty?
Book item: Look at the picture of some of the world's tallest statues. Identify the statues whose heights have the least difference.
Book item: Look at the picture of some of the world's tallest statues. Identify the statues whose heights have the largest difference.
Book item: Look at the picture of some of the world's tallest statues. The height of which statue will be equal to the height of the Statue of Unity, if it is doubled?

Book item: Measure 100 m and 200 m on your school playground, or any other place in and around your school, using a long tape. Mark these points and draw a straight line. Walk on the lines and count the number of steps. Use this relationship between the number of steps taken and distance walked to find distances around you for at least 3 locations. Wherever possible, walk and find the number of steps. Otherwise, find the distance and estimate the number of steps. (a): Identify and write the locations that are the nearest and the farthest from your home. (b): Write the distances obtained above in increasing order. (c): Name a location that is equal to or more than 1,000 m from your home.

Book item: Ropes of different lengths are used to make 1 km. Find how many ropes of each length are needed to make 1 km. A rope of 1,000 m: 1 rope. (a): a rope of 100 m: ___ ropes; (b): a rope of 10 m: ___ ropes; (c): a rope of 200 m: ___ ropes; (d): a rope of 500 m: ___ ropes; (e): a rope of 250 m: ___ ropes.

Book item: Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a 3 km race. Help them with the arrangements for the race. Water stations are to be arranged after every 500 m. How many water stations must be set up? At what positions from the starting point will these water stations be placed?

Book item: Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a 3 km race. Children need to stand at an interval of 300 m to direct the runners. How many children are needed? At what positions from the starting point will the children be standing?
Book item: Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a 3 km race. Red and blue flags are to be placed alternately at every 50 m. How many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?

Book item: The longest train journey in India is by The Vivek Express which runs from Dibrugarh in Assam to Kanniyakumari in Tamil Nadu. Look at the stations on the route shown in the table and answer. The total length of the route from Dibrugarh to Kanniyakumari is ___ km.
Book item: Look at the table of stations on the route of The Vivek Express from Dibrugarh. The distance between Vijayawada and Jalpaiguri Road is ___ km.
Book item: Look at the table of stations on the route of The Vivek Express from Dibrugarh. The distance between Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam is ___ km.
Book item: Look at the table of stations on the route of The Vivek Express from Dibrugarh. Which two stations are farther apart, Guwahati and Dimapur or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?
Book item: Look at the table of stations on the route of The Vivek Express from Dibrugarh. What is the distance between Guwahati and Coimbatore JN?
Book item: Let us look at the scale. Do you notice the small marks between 1 cm and 2 cm? Count how many marks there are between 1 cm and 2 cm.

Book item: Measure the lines in the design and write their measurements in cm and mm. The design has eight lines, each with an empty box beside it. In this question they are numbered from the top of the picture to the bottom: (1): the upper left slanting side of the large diamond; (2): the top side of the inner rectangle; (3): the right side of the big outer shape; (4): the right side of the inner rectangle; (5): the upper left side of the small tilted shape; (6): the lower left side of the small tilted shape; (7): the lower left slanting side of the large diamond; (8): the bottom side of the big outer shape.

Book item: Soak some seeds of whole moong or black or white chana overnight. Next morning, take them out and wrap them in a moist cloth to sprout them. Over the next 4 days, take out one seed each day and measure the length of sprout. For ease of measurement, you can either place the seed on a paper and mark the length of the sprout, or use a thread to find its length. Fill in the table: the length of the sprout in mm on Day 1, Day 2, Day 3 and Day 4.
Book item: Draw lines of the following lengths in your notebook using a scale. (a): 5 cm 5 mm; (b): 3 cm 6 mm; (c): 8 cm 3 mm; (d): 36 mm; (e): 67 mm.

Book item: Fill in the blanks appropriately in the double number line. Top line: 1 cm, 7 cm, 15 cm, ___ cm, ___ cm, ___ cm, 50 cm. Bottom line: 10 mm, ___ mm, ___ mm, 250 mm, 320 mm, 450 mm, ___ m. Fill in the two boxes ×___ as well: the arrow on the top line is ×7 and the arrow from the top line to the bottom line is ×10.

Book item: Fill in the blanks appropriately in the double number line. Top line: 1 m, 4 m, 10 m, ___ m, ___ m, ___ m, 21 m. Bottom line: ___ cm, ___ cm, ___ cm, 1,200 cm, 1,400 cm, 1,700 cm, ___ cm. Fill in the two boxes ×___ as well: the arrow on the top line is ×4 and the arrow from the top line to the bottom line is ×100.

Book item: Fill in the blanks appropriately in the double number line. Top line: 1 km, 9 km, 25 km, ___ km, ___ km, ___ km, 82 km. Bottom line: 1,000 m, ___ m, ___ m, 41,000 m, 55,000 m, 67,000 m, ___ m. Fill in the two boxes ×___ as well: the arrow on the top line is ×9 and the arrow from the top line to the bottom line is ×1,000.
Book item: Use your understanding from above to fill in the blanks appropriately. (a): 4 cm 5 mm = ___ mm; (b): 89 mm = ___ cm ___ mm; (c): 234 cm = ___ mm; (d): 514 mm = ___ cm ___ mm.

Book item: Use your understanding from above to fill in the blanks appropriately. (e): 6 m 34 cm = ___ cm; (f): 20 m 12 cm = ___ cm; (g): 397 m = ___ cm; (h): 5,792 cm = ___ m ___ cm; (i): 9,108 cm = ___ m ___ cm.

Book item: Use your understanding from above to fill in the blanks appropriately. (j): 34 km = ___ m; (k): 6,870 m = ___ km ___ m; (l): 10,552 m = ___ km ___ m; (m): 29 km 30 m = ___ m; (n): 32 km 359 m = ___ m.
Book item: Saji saw on his smartphone that he walked 3 km 450 m in the morning and another 4 km 650 m in the evening. How much did he walk in the whole day? How would you solve this problem?
Book item: Electricians are changing the cables in a house. They need 63 m of cable for this purpose. They used 16 m 75 cm cable in the first room. What is the length of the cable left?
Book item: Rani has two red coloured ribbon rolls, one of length 3 m 75 cm and another 2 m 25 cm long. How much ribbon does she have?
Book item: The distance from Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m. Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is on the way, and 17 km 900 m away from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?

Book item: Gulmarg Gondola in Gulmarg, Kashmir is the second longest and second highest cable car in the world. It is divided into two sections. The first section covers 2 km 300 m and the second section covers 2 km 650 m. What is the total distance covered by the cable car?
Book item: Circle the bigger length and find the difference. (a): 11 mm and 1 cm; (b): 26 mm and 2 cm; (c): 20 cm and 201 mm; (d): 1,020 mm and 1 m.
Book item: Circle the bigger length and find the difference. (e): 2 m and 245 cm; (f): 5,678 m and 6 km; (g): 6 km 1,480 m and 7 km 479 m.
Book item: We need a 1 m 80 cm cloth to make a shirt for a 10 year old child. How much cloth will be needed to make shirts for 20 such children?
Book item: A shop sells cloth for making bags at ₹100 for 5 m. How much money is needed to buy a 1 m cloth?

Book item: Now, use the double number line to find the cost of the cloth or the length of cloth that we can buy at a particular cost. Top line: 5 m, 10 m, 20 m, 40 m, ___ m. Bottom line: ₹100, ₹___, ₹___, ₹___, ₹2000. Fill in the four boxes ×___ as well.

Book item: Anita is making an embroidery on the border of a sari. She needs a 1 m long thread to embroider a 50 cm sari. How much thread would she need for a 5 m sari border? A 1 m long thread costs ₹50. How much money will be needed to buy the thread?
Book item: A road 12 km 600 m long is being laid in a town. The workers lay an equal length of road each day, and complete the work in 6 days. How much road laying work is done on each day?
Book item: Estimate the following. Share your reasoning in class. The height of the tallest building in your neighbourhood. What did you use as a reference to estimate the height?
Book item: Estimate the following. Share your reasoning in class. The height of the tallest tree in your neighbourhood. What did you use as a reference?
Book item: Estimate the following. Share your reasoning in class. The depth of a well or swimming pool in your neighbourhood. How did you find out?
Book item: Look at your ruler to see if inches are also marked on it. Find out how many cm and mm equal 1 inch.

Book item: Stand against a wall and mark your height. Measure the distance between the floor and the marked point in feet and inches. Similarly, other students in the class can also measure their heights. Find out who is the tallest student in your class. What is his or her height in feet and inches?
Book item: Put an appropriate operation sign (+, −, ×, ÷) in the empty boxes of the grid such that each row and column and each 2 × 2 box does not repeat the sign.

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter takes place in a village weaving centre with a long measuring tape on the wall, and on the roads, rulers and walls around it. Saris, stoles, ropes, trains, sprouts and statues are the lengths. Measuring them shows which unit fits, how one length has two names, and how to compare, add, subtract, multiply and divide lengths. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, builds and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Eight tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.
points.title: Videos teach, tools explore

points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.
points.title: A tool in three steps

points.text: Every solved example, Let Us Do question and every answerable prompt of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.
points.title: Every book question has its own video

points.text: Tapes, rulers, bars and double number lines carry each idea: equal marks, the length as the largest thing on screen, and the unit written beside every number.
points.title: The picture is the mathematics

points.text: Heights of statues, station distances, ropes, cloth prices and every question are the book's own. Any number the plan adds is a practice value and is said to be one.
points.title: Only the book's numbers
